sections.skill: Explain how investment gains and income are taxed and compare taxable and tax-advantaged accounts

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Leo bought shares for $2,000 and sold them for $2,600 in a taxable brokerage account. What is his capital gain?
questions.intro: A capital gain is the profit from selling an investment for more than its cost basis (what you paid, including some fees). In a taxable account, realized gains are generally taxable in the year you sell. A capital loss is the reverse.
sources: IRS (Topic 409, Capital Gains and Losses): Gains on assets held more than one year are generally long-term and taxed at lower rates (special rules apply to some assets); net capital losses can offset up to $3,000 of other income per year ($1,500 if married filing separately). (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc409)

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Under federal rules, a gain on an ordinary stock or fund investment in a taxable account held for MORE than one year is…

choices.text: short-term, taxed at ordinary income rates
long-term, usually taxed at lower rates
taxed only if it exceeds $1 million

questions.correct_answer: long-term, usually taxed at lower rates
questions.intro: For ordinary stock and fund investments in a taxable account, gains on investments held one year or less are short-term and taxed as ordinary income. Gains on investments held more than one year are long-term and generally taxed at lower rates (0%, 15%, or 20%, depending on income). Some assets, such as collectibles, have special rules.
questions.feedback: Holding more than one year generally makes the gain long-term, with lower rates.
sources: IRS (Topic 409, Capital Gains and Losses): Gains on assets held more than one year are generally long-term and taxed at lower rates (special rules apply to some assets); net capital losses can offset up to $3,000 of other income per year ($1,500 if married filing separately). (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc409)

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which account lets investments grow without yearly taxes on dividends and gains?

choices.text: A regular taxable brokerage account in her own name
A tax-advantaged retirement account such as an IRA

questions.correct_answer: A tax-advantaged retirement account such as an IRA
questions.intro: In a taxable brokerage account, dividends, most interest, and realized gains are generally taxed each year (some interest, such as on many municipal bonds, is exempt). Tax-advantaged accounts, such as IRAs and 401(k)s, let investments grow without yearly taxes; taxes are deferred (traditional) or avoided on qualified withdrawals (Roth).
questions.feedback: Retirement accounts shelter growth from yearly taxes.

misconceptions.A: Taxes due each year on distributions and sales

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Jo buys shares on March 1, 2025 and sells them at a gain on February 15, 2026. How is the gain treated?

choices.text: Long-term, since the sale is in a new calendar year
Long-term, since she held them close to a year
Short-term, since she held them one year or less
Tax-free, since she held them over six months

questions.correct_answer: Short-term, since she held them one year or less
questions.intro: A gain is long-term if the investment was held more than one year; otherwise it is short-term and taxed like ordinary income.
questions.feedback: March 1, 2025 to February 15, 2026 is less than a year, so the gain is short-term.
